title: Olmec Colossal Head 1: broad nose and full lips
observation: The Xalapa museum catalogs a broad nose and thick lips on its basalt head. The decorated upper section is identified separately as a headdress.
interpretation: Both features are visible in the frontal catalog photo.
limits: The artwork does not document skin color, hair texture, or the sitter’s ancestry.

sources.title: Coe, Diehl & Stuiver, excavation and dates

research.title: San Lorenzo Colossal Head 1
research.obs: The catalog notes a broad nose and full lips in basalt and describes a separate patterned headdress.
research.reading: The features can be checked in the photograph and compared across distinct Olmec works.
research.limits: Basalt does not document complexion. The headdress is not evidence of hair texture. Neither facial shape nor stone provenance identifies ancestry.
sources: Museo de Antropología de Xalapa, object 10958
Coe, Diehl & Stuiver, excavation and dates

title: Olmec Colossal Head 5: full, parted lips
observation: LACMA’s object guide identifies full, slightly parted lips with downturned corners on this San Lorenzo monument and labels its headgear separately.
interpretation: This is a documented visual feature of an individual work.
limits: The date range is an early San Lorenzo archaeological context, not a direct date of carving or of the person. The guide offers no tight-curl identification.

title: Veracruz figure: curls, or a curled hat?
observation: The Met’s ceramic figure shows curls around the head, with traces of white coloring. The museum identifies two readings: curled hair or a hat with curls.
interpretation: The sculpture clearly documents a curled form in pre-contact art.
limits: The catalog cannot distinguish hair from headwear. No verified tight natural curl identification follows from this object.

title: Brereton: a separate dark-olive encounter
observation: In a later encounter, Brereton describes a group with a dark-olive complexion. He separately mentions black hair worn long, tied behind in knots.
interpretation: A different observation from his latitude-43 account, not a second independent witness.
limits: The Buzzards Bay / Elizabeth Islands region is approximate. Neither complexion nor grooming establishes ancestry or natural curl pattern.

sources.title: Hakluyt Society excerpts at UC Davis

record.originalWording: of complexion or color, much like a dark olive
record.gloss: His English comparison is dark olive.
record.transmission: This is a later passage from the same 1602 voyage; phrasing varies slightly across editions.

title: William Wood: swarthy complexion and nose description
observation: Wood describes people in New England as darker in complexion than his Spanish comparison group. He separately mentions black hair and uses the term out-nosed.
interpretation: One description distinguishes complexion, hair color and nose shape. It does not say the nose is wide or that the hair is tightly curled.
limits: Wood generalized for a colonial readership. Publication year is not the date of a single encounter; the marker is a regional anchor.

record.sourceLocator: New Englands Prospect, Part II, ch. IV, p. 54
record.originalWording: of complexion something more swarthy than Spaniards … out-nosed
record.gloss: Darker in complexion than his Spanish comparison; out-nosed is a separate nose descriptor, plausibly prominent.

title: Lechford: swarthy complexion, paint noted separately
observation: Lechford describes complexion as swarthy and tawny. He notes black hair and ceremonial black and red face paint separately, and claims oil and coloring affected children's appearance.
interpretation: The source distinguishes his description of appearance from a separate description of paint.
limits: His beliefs about what caused the appearance are not demonstrated, and the paragraph is not a record of a single identified encounter.

record.sourceLocator: Of the Indians, original p. 50 / later edition p. 116
record.originalWording: They are of complexion swarthy and tawny
record.gloss: The author describes a dark or tawny complexion.
record.transmission: Read the following sentences for coloring, hair, and ceremonial paint.

title: Penn: ‘Black, but by design’ in context
observation: Penn uses the word Black but immediately qualifies it, attributing the darkness he saw to applied bear fat and exposure. He says the thick lips and flat noses he stereotyped as traits of other groups were not common among the people he describes.
interpretation: The full paragraph documents Penn’s vocabulary and perceptions. It does not corroborate that those features were prevalent.
limits: His causal claims and stereotypes are not established facts. This later colonial letter does not qualify for the direct complexion-only filter.

sources.title: Historical Society of Pennsylvania, 1683 letter excerpt

record.recordType: Letter to the Free Society of Traders
record.originalWording: Of Complexion, Black, but by design
record.gloss: Black in complexion, he claimed by deliberate practice.
record.transmission: The excerpt preserves the qualifier and explanation; do not quote Black in isolation.

title: Verrazzano: Carolina-area landfall
observation: After landing, Verrazzano explicitly describes complexion by comparison to Ethiopians, separately noting thick black hair tied back. He reports that the encounter was brief.
interpretation: This is an early surviving firsthand written description of people on the Atlantic coast as dark-complexioned. The manuscript's word for dark/black and the Ethiopia comparison are both significant.
limits: The landfall is usually placed near Cape Fear; the exact beach and community identity are uncertain. The comparison is not an identification of African ancestry.

record.sourceLocator: Cèllere Codex, fol. 2v; Wroth-based excerpt, p. 2
record.originalWording: sono di colori neri nò molto dagli Ethiopi disformi
record.gloss: Dark or black in color, not greatly unlike Ethiopians.
record.transmission: A contemporary Italian manuscript copy survives. Translation choices differ (‘dark’ versus ‘black’); retain the comparison and do not turn it into a population label.

sources.title: Critical Italian edition, §48 and preceding sections

title: Brereton: blacke swart complexion
observation: A participant in Gosnold’s voyage describes people who boarded the ship in coastal New England. He explicitly notes complexion and separately says their eyebrows were painted white.
interpretation: The wording is direct eyewitness evidence of how Brereton described the people he met. This is independent of Verrazzano's 1524 voyage.
limits: Exact anchorage uncertain: he reports latitude 43 degrees. Editions differ on the number of people boarding, but not on the description under study. This is not an ancestry claim.

record.sourceLocator: 1602 first edition, p. 4; second-impression transcription, p. 86
record.gloss: Of a black or very dark complexion; swart is an older word for dark.
record.transmission: First-impression wording is reproduced in a 1903 facsimile. A separate 1602 impression is excerpted by the Hakluyt Society; both preserve the key phrase.

sources.title: Hakluyt edition excerpt, pp. 144–145, UC Davis

title: Léry: natural complexion described as swarthy
observation: Léry expressly discusses natural complexion, compares the people he knew to Spaniards or Provençals, and discusses paint separately.
interpretation: The eyewitness gives an independent explicit swarthy-complexion description, with a different comparison from Verrazzano and Brereton.
limits: He qualifies the description, saying they are not otherwise black; the card is evidence for a swarthy description, not an explicit identification as Black.

record.sourceLocator: Histoire d’un voyage, ch. VIII, printed pp. 109–110
record.originalWording: n’estans pas autrement noirs, ils sont seulement basanez
record.gloss: Not otherwise black, they are only swarthy or tanned.
record.transmission: Original Early Modern French edition, digitized by the University of Tours; English gloss here is literal, not a standardized skin-color category.

title: Baegert: Baja California, later comparison
observation: A resident missionary describes skin colors ranging from dark chestnut or clove-brown to nearly black among some people, and tawny or copper-red among others.
interpretation: It is a direct description of variation among people the author writes about in the Baja California mission era.
limits: This is more than two centuries later than Verrazzano and is not a first-contact or pre-contact record. The author’s causal beliefs and colonial judgments are not adopted.

record.originalWording: sticht aber bey einigen mehr auf schwarz
record.gloss: But in some it tends more toward black.
record.transmission: Original German scan and English edition supplied; use the original to check translation.

title: Guanahani: complexion versus paint
status: Context only; not a dark-skin match
observation: Columbus distinguishes reported complexion from paint. He compares complexion to Canary Islanders and describes dark, white and red paint as applied.
interpretation: This is a useful control for reading a term in its sentence rather than accepting a color-word search hit.
limits: The island identification is debated. The surviving text is Las Casas’s later abstract, not Columbus’s autograph. The passage does not explicitly document Black skin.

record.observer: Christopher Columbus, as transmitted by Bartolomé de las Casas
record.recordType: Voyage diary transcribed and abridged later
record.originalWording: de la color de los canarios, ni negros ni blancos
record.gloss: Of the color of Canary Islanders, neither black nor white.
record.transmission: Read the two entries together: the dark paint and the complexion comparison are separate descriptions.

sources.title: Spanish Diario, Early Modern Spain edition

title: Caminha: reddish-brown versus applied pigment
status: Context only; not a dark-skin match
observation: At Porto Seguro, Caminha describes the complexion of two men taken aboard using pardos and a reddish modifier, and their hair as straight. He records body painting separately.
interpretation: The same account is useful for distinguishing a color adjective from painted skin or hair texture.
limits: This reddish-brown description is not counted as explicit dark or black complexion. Later official meanings of pardo should not be projected back onto the sentence.

record.sourceLocator: Passage immediately after Afonso Lopes brings two men aboard
record.gloss: Brownish, somewhat reddish (modernized Portuguese spelling in the reading edition).
record.transmission: Portuguese archive transcript and modernized reading edition; find the two men boarding for the exact passage.

title: Verrazzano: sailor’s Cape Lookout account
observation: Verrazzano credits a young sailor who went ashore with a dark complexion and glossy-skin description, on a separate leg of the same voyage.
interpretation: The report records a second encounter, but Verrazzano attributes this observation to his crew member.
limits: Not a second independent author or Verrazzano’s direct observation. A later coastal encounter in the same letter gives a varied bronze-to-tawny comparison; do not merge the encounters.

record.observer: Unnamed sailor, reported by Giovanni da Verrazzano
record.recordType: Crew observation related in expedition letter
record.sourceLocator: Cèllere Codex, fol. 4v; critical edition §48; Wroth excerpt pp. 3–4
record.originalWording: sono di colore nero come gl’altri
record.gloss: They are dark or black in color like the others.
record.transmission: Italian text and translated excerpt transmit the sailor’s report; it is not direct first-person testimony by the letter’s author.

sources.title: Critical Italian edition, §48 and preceding sections

title: White Sands footprints
observation: Human tracks are preserved in ancient lake-margin deposits. The original aquatic-seed dates were checked using terrestrial pollen radiocarbon and quartz luminescence; a later study added a separate mud-dating record.
interpretation: The studies support humans present in present-day New Mexico about 23,000–21,000 years ago, well before Clovis.
limits: Methods date surrounding materials. The tracks do not identify the first arrival, skin color, population, migration route, or a present-day nation.

sources.title: Bennett et al., original footprint study
Pigati et al., independent age estimates
Holliday et al., independent sediment chronology

research.title: White Sands footprints
research.obs: Human footprints occur in layers of a former lake margin. Aquatic seeds were dated first; terrestrial pollen, luminescence and later sediment work tested the chronology.
research.reading: Human presence in present-day New Mexico substantially predates the Clovis archaeological horizon.
research.limits: The materials around the tracks are dated, not the trackmakers. The tracks do not identify ancestry, complexion or the first route of entry.

title: Swan Point
observation: An early cultural layer includes microblades and other artifacts; a study dated and traced an associated mammoth tusk.
interpretation: People occupied this region of what is now Alaska roughly 14,000 years ago.
limits: The tusk and site association do not demonstrate a mammoth kill or establish an exclusive migration path.

sources.title: Alaska Office of History and Archaeology
Rowe et al., mammoth and early Alaskan settlement

research.title: Swan Point
research.obs: The early cultural layer includes microblade tools and associated materials. Researchers dated and analyzed an associated mammoth tusk.
research.reading: People occupied this part of Alaska around 14,000 years ago and worked a range of materials.
research.limits: Associated ivory does not demonstrate a kill event or fix an entry date for the Americas.

title: Monte Verde II
observation: The excavation team identified cultural deposits and reported an age around 14,500 calibrated years before present. In 2026 another team proposed a much younger age, 8,200–4,200 years before present, from regional stratigraphy and volcanic ash correlation.
interpretation: The original team disputes the revised stratigraphic correlation and continues to defend its timeline. The slider window covers both proposals; it is not evidence of continuous occupation.
limits: The age dispute turns on whether strata correlate across locations and whether material was redeposited. Neither interpretation resolves settlement elsewhere.

sources.title: Dillehay et al., excavation team's response

research.title: Monte Verde II
research.obs: The excavators defend approximately 14,500 years. A 2026 analysis proposed a middle-Holocene date from regional sediment correlation and volcanic ash.
research.reading: Two distinct interpretations are in active dispute. Compare their stratigraphic arguments and treatment of redeposited material.
research.limits: The CSV range spans rival proposals, not continuous occupation. Neither position resolves the dates of other sites.

title: San Lorenzo colossal heads
observation: Individualized faces and headgear are visible; descriptions note full lips and other facial details. Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology identifies carving and a possible reused throne feature on Head 2. Five of six radiocarbon results in an original excavation report cluster about 1200–900 BCE.
interpretation: One archaeological interpretation is that some heads portray local rulers. Ivan Van Sertima proposed African contact partly from visual parallels. A published critique identifies chronology and provenance problems with that reading.
limits: The displayed date range is an early excavation context, not a direct date for every object. Carved shape is worth recording; unpigmented basalt does not preserve skin color, and resemblance alone cannot distinguish local depiction, stylistic convention, or ancestry. Local stone provenance does not itself establish who is depicted.

sources.title: Coe, Diehl & Stuiver, excavation and dates
Van Sertima, They Came Before Columbus

title: Anzick burial genomic study
observation: The study sequenced an individual buried in association with Clovis artifacts in what is now Montana, dated to roughly 12,600 years ago.
interpretation: The sampled individual showed close genetic relationships with Indigenous American populations studied, contributing to models of population history.
limits: One individual cannot represent all earlier groups, identify White Sands trackmakers, prove an exact migration route, or determine modern citizenship. No genetic files or precise burial coordinates are reproduced.

sources.title: Moreno-Mayar et al., wider ancient genomes

research.title: Anzick-1
research.obs: Researchers analyzed the genome of one individual buried with Clovis-associated objects.
research.reading: Comparisons support close population relationships with sampled Indigenous American populations.
research.limits: One genome does not represent every ancient population or identify the White Sands trackmakers. It cannot determine modern citizenship.

title: Upward Sun River genomic study
observation: Researchers sequenced a roughly 11,500-year-old genome from central Alaska and compared it with other published genomes.
interpretation: The analysis identified an early branch the authors termed Ancient Beringians and modeled relationships among sampled groups.
limits: The label names a sampled genetic branch, not a modern nation or a claim about the identity of earlier footprint makers. Estimates depend on samples and models.

title: Oneida Indian Nation: Origins
observation: The Oneida Indian Nation publishes its own account of origins, including the Sky Woman creation story and the Nation’s enduring relationship with its Central New York homelands.
interpretation: Read alongside material and written records as a distinct source of knowledge, in the Nation’s own terms.
limits: No archaeological date is assigned. This is not a pan-Indigenous account, a genetic claim, or a license to republish protected knowledge.

sources.title: Global Indigenous Data Alliance, CARE Principles

title: Polynesian–Indigenous American contact
observation: Present-day and ancient-genome studies report independently supported pre-European gene flow between Polynesian and Indigenous American populations.
interpretation: This is a comparison case for the kind of corroboration that can support a contact hypothesis. The pin marks Rapa Nui, a study location, not a proposed American landfall.
limits: Models and date estimates differ; the entry does not pin down route or who voyaged, nor does it support a separate African–Olmec contact claim.

sources.title: Moreno-Mayar et al., ancient Rapanui genomes

research.title: Polynesian–Indigenous American contact
research.place: Rapa Nui study anchor; landfall unresolved
research.dates: Estimated contact in the centuries before European arrival
research.obs: Modern and ancient-genome studies report Indigenous American ancestry in Polynesian populations that predates sustained European contact.
research.reading: Multiple studies support trans-Pacific contact, advancing an independently testable hypothesis.
research.limits: The find does not identify the boat, voyage direction or exact landfall, and does not support a separate transatlantic contact claim.
sources: Moreno-Mayar et al., ancient Rapanui genomes

title: L’Anse aux Meadows
observation: Three pieces of worked wood from the excavated Norse site contained a known cosmic-ray marker; tree rings date the cutting to 1021 CE.
interpretation: A benchmark for how independent dating and diagnostic material can establish a specific overseas presence. This entry is an explicit exception to the pre-European-contact filter, included for comparison.
limits: This is not the precise first landing date and does not demonstrate African contact or rewrite Indigenous histories.

sources.title: Kuitems et al., evidence for European presence in 1021 CE

research.title: Norse activity at L’Anse aux Meadows
research.obs: Three worked-wood samples preserve a known atmospheric radiocarbon event and enough annual rings to locate the year of cutting.
research.reading: The site documents Norse activity in North America in 1021 CE, centuries before Columbus.
research.limits: It does not identify the first or last visit or document a specific meeting with an Indigenous community.

title: Cahokia
observation: Monumental earthworks, plazas and settlement traces document large-scale construction and a connected town-and-farm landscape.
interpretation: A major Mississippian urban center grew rapidly around the middle of the 11th century. Isotope studies suggest some individuals grew up elsewhere.
limits: Earthwork volume is not a census. An isotope value does not identify an individual's nation or language.

title: Pueblo Bonito
observation: Ancestral Pueblo people built a large masonry complex over several centuries. Laboratory analysis found a cacao marker in sampled cylinder jar fragments.
interpretation: The architecture shows sustained planning and labor. Cacao is material evidence for long-distance exchange with warmer-growing regions.
limits: The study does not trace a single trade route or identify the use of every room and vessel.

title: The Great Law of Peace
observation: The Confederacy describes its original five nations, their own councils and the common Grand Council. Clan Mothers select chiefs.
interpretation: The account documents how the Confederacy explains its own governance, peace and authority.
limits: The exact founding date is not settled. This is not a chronology for other Indigenous nations or a model of modern electoral government.

title: Thule sites in the western Canadian Arctic
observation: Radiocarbon measurements at Nelson River and Washout were used to reassess the tempo of eastward Thule movement.
interpretation: The authors argue that eastward movement began around the 13th century. Additional work documents local Thule occupation on Somerset Island.
limits: These dates are not the date of first Arctic occupation. Arctic communities predate this particular expansion.

title: Early maize in the Central Balsas
observation: Starch grains and phytoliths associated with tools and sediments were identified as maize; companion excavations reported contextual dates.
interpretation: The plant evidence places maize in use in this area by roughly 8,700 calibrated years ago.
limits: This is not the date of first cultivation everywhere, a recovered intact cob, or evidence of dependence on maize.

observation: Some cob genomes in this time window show close relationships with South American maize strains.
interpretation: The authors infer a northward movement of crop lineages in addition to earlier dispersals south.
limits: Plant genetics do not identify the people who carried the crop or their ancestry.

observation: A long artificial plateau and multiple causeways were documented by lidar and excavations.
interpretation: A large construction project was undertaken early in Maya-region history, implying coordinated labor.
limits: A monumental platform does not establish a ruler, exact population, or absence of social hierarchy.

title: Corriental reservoir at Tikal
observation: Researchers identified zeolite and quartz in dated reservoir layers.
interpretation: The authors infer that people procured the minerals for water filtration, an example of engineering with local water constraints.
limits: The filter hardware and operating details are not preserved. This is evidence from one reservoir, not every Maya city.

interpretation: Some results support migration into this urban district, adding evidence for mobility within the city's population.
limits: The sample is not a census. Isotope ranges can overlap and do not name an ethnicity or precise birthplace.

limits: Dating bark is not the same as dating ink. This dossier does not assign a map pin or a precise year of writing.

title: Tlaxcallan and Tizatlán
observation: One excavation-based interpretation emphasizes dispersed plazas and participatory or collective government. Later fieldwork reassesses the evidence for elite residences or palaces.
interpretation: Different political arrangements were possible within Mesoamerica; the expected buildings can test competing models.
limits: Architecture does not prove universal participation, modern suffrage, or the complete absence of elites.

limits: The sample date range is not a founding date for all coastal Peru; it does not tell us the exact political system.

sources: Harlow et al., original materials study

title: Tibes ceremonial center
observation: Excavations recorded formal plazas and ball courts. A cluster of dated samples suggests a major phase of reorganization.
interpretation: Communities built and maintained shared ceremonial and public spaces before sustained European colonization.
limits: The date cluster does not directly date every court or rule out earlier structures.

title: Networks and continuity in the Caribbean
observation: The study recovered 174 authenticated new genomes and compared them with other data. Results show movement and relationships among some sampled island populations.
interpretation: Patterns of continuity across some pottery changes caution against treating every change in style as a new migration.
limits: The youngest samples can postdate contact. Genetic groupings are not citizenship, national identity, or a diagnosis of ancestry for any modern individual.

title: Chegeree maps the Ohio–Mississippi corridor
observation: A manuscript map credited to Chegeree shows settlements, rivers, distances, and French posts from Lake Erie to the mouth of the Ohio.
interpretation: Indigenous geographic knowledge is visible in a record that also served British military interests. The Library of Congress describes the date as circa 1755.
limits: Chegeree’s nation is unconfirmed. This map neither covers the lower Mississippi delta nor establishes a border or control.

sources.title: Library of Congress: manuscript map and catalog
Library of Congress: Indigenous cartography guide

title: Cecilia petitions for Naneta’s freedom
observation: Cecilia’s surviving petition, dated January 10, 1798, argued for her niece Naneta’s freedom based on Indigenous maternal descent. She sought purchase of her freedom as an alternative. The March 15, 1798 order directed the appointment of appraisers.
interpretation: This case records a family’s challenge to enslavement under Spanish colonial law. The K4BL edition identifies Cecilia as Afro-Indigenous. Louisiana Historical Center file 1124 is indexed 1793-08-07-01; that is not the date of the surviving petition or order.
limits: The order does not establish that Naneta was freed. This is evidence about a particular family, not a general ancestry claim. The pin marks the proceeding, not the family’s residence.

title: Caddo treaty at the Agency House
observation: The treaty was signed July 1, 1835 and ratified February 2, 1836. The Caddo Nation identifies the signers as Northwestern Louisiana Caddo under principal chief Tsauninot.
interpretation: Read the U.S. treaty manuscript alongside the Nation’s account of the removal of multiple bands and their later reunion.
limits: The agreement does not identify an all-Caddo homeland or imply all Caddo bands signed. Place marker is approximate near present-day Shreveport.

sources.title: National Archives treaty manuscript via Indigenous Digital Archive

title: New Echota treaty and Cherokee protest
observation: A treaty was signed at New Echota in 1835. John Ross’s protest challenged its authority and described how commissioners treated absence as assent.
interpretation: Read the treaty against the protest, not as a single account of Cherokee consent.
limits: The protest documents the objection to the process; it does not mean the Cherokee Nation was invented by the United States.

title: Fort Laramie and the Black Hills taking
observation: Article XII specified signatures from three-quarters of adult male Indians affected by a cession. The Supreme Court’s account says the later agreement had roughly one-tenth, amid a congressional cutoff of subsistence unless the Sioux ceded the Black Hills.
interpretation: Congress enacted the taking in 1877 despite the signature threshold. The 1980 opinion reconstructs that sequence.
limits: The treaty and court opinion are distinct source types; the signature rule must not be generalized to negotiations with other Nations.

sources.title: United States v. Sioux Nation, pages 381–384
